title: Productivity and Costs, First Quarter 2026, Revised
date_evidence: BLS Productivity and Costs news release archive filename prod2_05072026 (released 7 May 2026); "Productivity up 0.3 percent in first quarter 2026"
key_claim: U.S. nonfarm business sector labor productivity (output per hour) increased 0.3 percent in the first quarter of 2026; over the current business cycle from Q4 2019 through Q1 2026 productivity has grown at an annualized 2.1 percent, above the 1.5 percent rate of the previous cycle and equal to the long-run 2.1 percent rate since 1947.
frame_summary: Official US data show aggregate labour productivity rose only modestly in early 2026, with no economy-wide surge that would corroborate firm-level claims of transformational AI productivity gains.
notes: Tier 1 macro anchor: aggregate productivity barely moved, tensioning the decoupling premise.

publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (Liberty Street Economics)
title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor-Market Effects of AI?
date_evidence: "The post was published on May 14, 2026, by Richard Audoly, Miles Guerin, and Giorgio Topa"; URL path /2026/05/
key_claim: Evidence from job postings provides little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand; while AI may be contributing to recent developments, it is not the main driver of the hiring slowdown, which reflects interest rates, post-pandemic overhiring and a weak labor backdrop, with weakness concentrated in the tech sector.
frame_summary: New York Fed economists argue the 2026 hiring slowdown is driven mainly by rates, overhiring and tech-sector retrenchment rather than by AI hollowing out labour demand.
notes: Tier 1 counter-anchor: the measured labour-market effect of AI is still weak/ambiguous.

title: AI reshapes global labour market into two distinct paths: 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer
key_claim: Analysing more than one billion job ads across 27 countries, PwC found companies in the most AI-exposed sectors recorded 34 percent productivity (revenue per employee) growth in 2025 relative to 2018 versus 24 percent for the least exposed, with the top 20 percent of AI-exposed firms achieving 163 percent productivity growth; headcount growth at the most AI-exposed companies outpaced the least exposed (52 percent vs 36 percent) and the average wage premium for AI skills reached 62 percent, while AI-skill job postings grew about eight times (69 percent) faster than the overall jobs market (9 percent).
frame_summary: PwC argues AI is producing a productivity boom concentrated in a minority of AI-exposed firms, which are growing both productivity and headcount faster than their peers rather than shrinking employment.
notes: Tier 2: the bullish productivity case; also shows gains and headcount growth concentrate in a minority, undercutting average-firm cuts.

title: Autonomous Business and AI Layoffs May Create Budget Room but Do Not Deliver Returns
date_evidence: Gartner press release slug 2026-05-05-gartner-says-...-do-not-deliver-returns; corroborated by Computerworld report dated "May 5, 2026": "according to new Gartner research"
key_claim: In a Gartner survey of 350 global business leaders at large organisations already using AI agents and automation, 80 percent reported lowered headcount as a result of AI initiatives (in some cases by up to 20 percent), yet Gartner found no correlation between achieving ROI and layoffs, with some firms forced to quickly rehire; Gartner expects roughly 6 million roles to be automated globally between 2023 and 2029 but predicts AI-created jobs will outpace those lost by 2029, with around 32 million workers a year seeing their roles transformed.
frame_summary: Gartner argues that cutting headcount on AI delivers no measurable ROI advantage over firms that cut less, and that workforce reduction is the wrong primary metric for AI value.
notes: Tier 2 core counter: layoffs uncorrelated with ROI; some firms forced to rehire. Date corroborated via Computerworld (05/05/2026).

title: Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity
date_evidence: URL path /blog/2026-05-11-ai-usage-survey/ ; METR blog dated 11 May 2026
key_claim: METR cautions that survey results on AI productivity are not necessarily grounded in reality and that especially high self-reported value estimates are plausibly overstated, consistent with earlier findings that people overestimated AI's effect on their task time by around 40 percentage points on average, so self-reported productivity gains should be treated sceptically.
frame_summary: METR, an AI-evaluations research organisation, argues that self-reported AI productivity gains are unreliable and likely overstated, so firms should not treat them as proven.
notes: Tier 2 counter on measurement: the productivity self-reports underpinning cuts are unreliable.

title: AI will boost productivity so ServiceNow won't have to backfill open jobs, CEO says
date_evidence: CNBC URL path /2026/04/22/servicenow-mcdermott-ai-jobs-earnings.html ; report of ServiceNow Q1 2026 earnings remarks (22 April 2026)
key_claim: ServiceNow CEO Bill McDermott said the company expects to begin 2027 with roughly the same total headcount it had at the start of 2026, even while integrating acquisitions, because AI-driven productivity means it does not have to backfill attrition; the company is positioning AI to decouple revenue growth from headcount, targeting around $300 million in hard cost reductions in 2026 on flat headcount.
frame_summary: ServiceNow's CEO presents flat headcount and no backfilling of attrition as a deliberate strategy to grow revenue without growing employment, using AI productivity.
notes: Tier 3: the live corporate example of revenue-headcount decoupling as explicit guidance.

title: Tech Layoffs Hit 1,115 a Day in 2026: Companies Cite AI but Cuts Fail to Boost Returns
date_evidence: Tech Times URL path /20260616/ ; headline "Tech Layoffs Hit 1,115 a Day in 2026" (16 June 2026)
key_claim: Tech layoffs in 2026 are running at about 1,115 job cuts per day, nearly double the previous year's pace, with companies including Meta, Oracle and Block citing artificial intelligence to justify eliminating roles, even as the cuts are reported to be failing to boost financial returns.
frame_summary: Tech Times reports that AI-cited tech layoffs accelerated sharply in 2026 while failing to translate into stronger returns.
notes: Tier 3 scale/corroboration of the headcount reset and the returns gap; treat figures directionally.
